The two size pairs are genuinely converted, not raw feet (2-7 ft to 24-84 in, 3-5 ft to 36-60 in), both from the single species-level Dimensions block on NC State, with min <= max and both ends on the page; RHS's own structured Max Height 1.5-2.5 m and Max Spread 1-1.5 m independently corroborate them. is_edible=false is a real denial from two sources (NC State 'The fruits are poisonous and can cause cardiac arrest if ingested in large quantities', plus 'Poisonous to Humans'; RHS 'Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten'), not silence. attracts_pollinators=true rests on RHS's per-plant 'Plants for pollinators' recognition badge, which is markup attached to this taxon and names pollinators -- and the researcher correctly declined to lean on NC State's 'Attracts birds' / 'Songbirds', which would have been the bogus support. All four citations are labelled with the literal field names and all four quotes verify verbatim as single rendered runs, no U+23CE and no label glued across a newline. The mobot ConnectError is real and honestly recorded. The one defect worth fixing is documentation only: the unknowns entry about RHS claims there is no structured Ultimate height/spread field and treats the 0.5m-7m narrative as a sharp conflict, when RHS does publish a structured Size block whose numbers agree with the accepted values. That note should be rewritten; no field value changes.

unknowns: RHS (both the mahonia-aquifolium/10730 and berberis-aquifolium/68984 detail pages, which render identical content) gives a smaller size than NC State: Max Height 0.5-1 metres (~19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (~39.4-59.1 in). This conflicts with NC State's Height 3-6 ft / Width 2-5 ft. NC State's structured Dimensions block was used as the size anchor per instructions; the RHS figures were not merged in.

is_edible is TRUE but conditional: NC State tags the species '#edible fruits' and lists Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible, but its Edibility note says the berries are 'Not poisonous, but ... contain berberine that can cause stomach upset, especially with children.' So the fruit is edible but should not be eaten in quantity, especially by children.

is_edible removed on audit: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/berberis-aquifolium/) does not merely qualify the fruit — it carries a full "Poisonous to Humans" block naming toxic parts: "Poison Part:" with values Bark, Leaves, Roots and Sap/Juice, alongside "Poison Severity: Low", "Poison Symptoms: Ingestion may cause minor illnesses such as vomiting or diarrhea.", "Poison Toxic Principle: Berberine, a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid", the structured "Plant Type: ... Poisonous" value, and the tag "#poisonous if ingested". The record's unknowns disclose only the berry caveat (berries contain berberine, stomach upset, especially children); they never state that four plant parts are listed as poison parts or that the plant is typed Poisonous. A page naming toxic parts while is_edible is true requires that condition in unknowns, and it is absent, so is_edible is nulled. To restore it, unknowns must carry the Poison Part list (Bark, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice) and the "Ingestion may cause minor illnesses such as vomiting or diarrhea" symptom line, not just the berry note.

landed.summary: Re-read all four pages with qc.py. The three size/pollinator fields hold up: NC State's single species-level Dimensions block reads "Height: 3 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in." and "Width: 2 ft. 0 in. - 5 ft. 0 in.", which convert exactly to the recorded 36-72 and 24-60 inches, and every quote in the record is on its page verbatim as one rendered run. attracts_pollinators is supported by named pollinators on both sources (RHS "Plants for pollinators", NC State "Attracts: Pollinators" and tag "#pollinator plant"), not by birds or generic wildlife prose. Mobot genuinely refuses (error:ConnectError), and the RHS/NC State size conflict is disclosed rather than silently merged. The defect is is_edible: NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" block names Poison Part: Bark, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice (plus Plant Type: Poisonous and tag #poisonous if ingested), and none of that reaches unknowns, which mention only the berry/berberine stomach-upset caveat.
